claim.text: For sparse training of a model from a random initialization independent of the initialization used to discover the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) mask $\mathfrak{m}_A$, using the permuted mask $\pi(\mathfrak{m}_A)$ yields consistently higher test accuracy than using the non-permuted mask $\mathfrak{m}_A$ across architectures, datasets, sparsity levels $S\in\{0.80,0.90,0.95,0.97\}$, and rewind points $k$ (the epoch from which weights are reset before sparse training).

For sparse training of a model from a random initialization independent of the initialization used to discover the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) mask $\mathfrak{m}_A$, the LTH baseline (training the original initialization with $\mathfrak{m}_A$ after weight rewinding) serves as an upper bound on test accuracy.

For sparse training of a model from a random initialization independent of the initialization used to discover the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) mask $\mathfrak{m}_A$, on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ResNet20, the permuted solution (using the permuted mask $\pi(\mathfrak{m}_A)$) outperforms the naive solution (using the non-permuted mask $\mathfrak{m}_A$) at all four sparsity levels $S\in\{0.80,0.90,0.95,0.97\}$ and all tested rewind points $k\in\{0,5,10,15,20,25,50,75,100\}$.

For sparse training of a model from a random initialization independent of the initialization used to discover the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) mask $\mathfrak{m}_A$, on CIFAR-10 with VGG11, the permuted solution (using the permuted mask $\pi(\mathfrak{m}_A)$) outperforms the naive solution (using the non-permuted mask $\mathfrak{m}_A$) at all tested rewind points $k\in\{0,5,10,15,20,25,50\}$ for 80% and 90% sparsity.
For ResNet20×1 on CIFAR-10 at 90% sparsity and $k=75$, permuted test accuracy is 90.03% versus naive 88.81% and LTH 91.36%;

For sparse training of a model from a random initialization independent of the initialization used to discover the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) mask $\mathfrak{m}_A$, the permuted solution (using the permuted mask $\pi(\mathfrak{m}_A)$) reduces the accuracy gap between the LTH baseline (training the original initialization with $\mathfrak{m}_A$ after weight rewinding) and the naive solution (using the non-permuted mask $\mathfrak{m}_A$) from 2.55 to 1.33 percentage points for ResNet20×1 on CIFAR-10 at 90% sparsity and $k=75$.

For sparse training of a model from a random initialization independent of the initialization used to discover the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) mask $\mathfrak{m}_A$, on ImageNet with ResNet50 at 90% sparsity and $k=25$, the permuted Top-1 accuracy (using the permuted mask $\pi(\mathfrak{m}_A)$) is 66.37% while the naive Top-1 accuracy (using the non-permuted mask $\mathfrak{m}_A$) is 64.77%, a difference of 1.6 percentage points.

For sparse training of a model from a random initialization independent of the initialization used to discover the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) mask $\mathfrak{m}_A$, on ImageNet with ResNet50 at 95% sparsity and $k=25$, the permuted Top-1 accuracy (using the permuted mask $\pi(\mathfrak{m}_A)$) is 62.77% while the naive Top-1 accuracy (using the non-permuted mask $\mathfrak{m}_A$) is 60.77%, a difference of 2.0 percentage points.

Across repeated runs at 90% sparsity, ensembles formed from independently trained permuted-mask models exhibit larger function-space diversity than ensembles of Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) models retrained with the same mask $\mathfrak{m}_A$ and initialization with 5 different data orders.
For ResNet20×1 on CIFAR-10, the permuted ensemble accuracy is 91.75% versus LTH ensemble 91.43%
For ResNet20×1 on CIFAR-10, the LTH (Lottery Ticket Hypothesis) single-model mean accuracy is higher than the permuted-mask single-model mean accuracy: 91.15% versus 89.38%.
; disagreement is 0.107 for permuted vs 0.035 for LTH
, KL divergence is 0.273 vs 0.038,
JS divergence is 0.091 vs 0.011.
For ResNet20×4 on CIFAR-100, the permuted ensemble accuracy is 77.85% versus LTH ensemble 75.99%
; disagreement is 0.278 for permuted vs 0.117 for LTH
, KL divergence is 0.918 vs 0.134,
JS divergence is 0.327 vs 0.038.

After correcting interpolation-induced variance collapse via the REPAIR (REnormalizing Permuted Activations for Interpolation Repair) renormalization, the loss barrier $\mathcal{B}(\theta_1,\theta_2)$ (defined as $\sup_{\alpha\in[0,1]}[\mathcal{L}((1-\alpha)\theta_1+\alpha\theta_2)-((1-\alpha)\mathcal{L}(\theta_1)+\alpha\mathcal{L}(\theta_2))]$) between a dense trained solution $\mathbf{w}_A^{t=T}$ (model $A$ trained to convergence) and the corresponding sparse LTH (Lottery Ticket Hypothesis) solution (obtained by retraining the original initialization with mask $\mathfrak{m}_A$ after weight rewinding) remains small across iterative magnitude pruning iterations even at high sparsity.

After correcting interpolation-induced variance collapse via the REPAIR (REnormalizing Permuted Activations for Interpolation Repair) renormalization, the result in claim 19 demonstrates linear mode connectivity modulo variance collapse.

For ResNet20×4 on CIFAR-10 at 90% sparsity, the error barrier between the dense trained solution and the corresponding sparse LTH (Lottery Ticket Hypothesis) solution after applying REPAIR (REnormalizing Permuted Activations for Interpolation Repair) is near zero across iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) iterations.
The quality of activation-based permutation matching improves as network layer widths increase.
As network layer widths increase, smaller interpolation loss barriers between permuted and independently trained dense models are produced.
As network layer widths increase, permuted-mask sparse training results that approach the LTH (Lottery Ticket Hypothesis) baseline for wider models are yielded.
For ResNet20 on CIFAR-10 with width multipliers $w\in\{1,4,8,16\}$, the loss barrier after permutation and REPAIR (REnormalizing Permuted Activations for Interpolation Repair) decreases with width.

For ResNet20 on CIFAR-10 with width multipliers $w\in\{1,4,8,16\}$, at 90% sparsity and rewind point $k=75$, the gap between the permuted test accuracy and the LTH (Lottery Ticket Hypothesis) test accuracy shrinks from 1.33 percentage points to 0.01 percentage points as the width multiplier increases from $w=1$ to $w=16$.
Similar trends to those in claim 22, claim 23, claim 24 are observed on CIFAR-100.

It is feasible to compute the activation-matching permutation $\pi$ by aligning a fully trained model $A$ (trained to convergence, $T=200$ epochs) to an early checkpoint $\mathbf{w}_B^{t=i}$ of the target model $B$ ($i\in\{5,20,50,100\}$), and using that $\pi$ to permute the mask for sparse training of model $B$ from rewind point $k=20$.
For ResNet20×1 on CIFAR-10, full matching at 95% sparsity yields 88.29% test accuracy,
early matching at $t=5$ yields 87.37%,
at $t=20$ yields 87.68%,
at $t=50$ yields 87.43%,
at $t=100$ yields 87.54%;
For ResNet20×1 on CIFAR-10, at 95% sparsity, all early-matching permuted solutions outperform the naive baseline (87.31% test accuracy).
At 90% sparsity, full matching yields 89.50%,
early matching at $t=5$ yields 89.16%
At 80% sparsity, full matching yields 90.68%,
early matching at $t=5$ yields 90.49%
Permutations obtained by matching to early training iterations enable the permuted solution to outperform the naive baseline at typical rewind points.

For sparse training of a model from a random initialization independent of the initialization used to discover the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) mask $\mathfrak{m}_A$, using the permuted mask $\pi(\mathfrak{m}_A)$ yields consistently higher test accuracy than using the non-permuted mask $\mathfrak{m}_A$ across the architectures ResNet20, VGG11, and ResNet50, the datasets CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, sparsity levels $S\in\{0.80,0.90,0.95,0.97\}$, and rewind points $k$ (the epoch from which weights are reset before sparse training).

note.text: elaboration of claim 9: The permuted ensemble uses 5 different permutations of the same mask $\mathfrak{m}_A$ with 5 different random weight initializations; the LTH ensemble uses the same mask and initialization with 5 different data orders.

elaboration of claim 9: Diversity is measured by disagreement (fraction of test samples where predictions differ), Kullback–Leibler divergence (average KL divergence between predicted distributions), and Jensen–Shannon divergence (average JS divergence between predicted distributions).
